title: Methotrexate and Alcohol: Can You Drink? Liver Risks and Limits
excerpt: Can you drink on methotrexate? How methotrexate and alcohol affect your liver, what rheumatology and dermatology guidance says about limits, dose-day timing, and warning signs to watch for.
metaDescription: Can you drink on methotrexate? How methotrexate and alcohol affect your liver, how much is too much, dose-day timing, and warning signs to watch for.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** whether you can drink at all on methotrexate is your prescriber's call, not something to decide from an article. Methotrexate and alcohol can both scar the liver, and the damage adds up quietly without symptoms. Some doctors allow an occasional small amount of alcohol for people on low-dose weekly methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, or psoriatic arthritis, as long as liver blood tests stay normal. Others, and some dermatology guidelines, prefer that you avoid alcohol entirely, especially if you have other liver risk factors. Where drinking is allowed, the rules are about *how much* you drink across the whole week. Your prescriber's advice beats anything in a general article, including this one.

**The quick rules:** Ask your prescriber how much alcohol, if any, is acceptable for you, and stick to that number. If they're comfortable with some drinking, keep it light and spread out, never binge, and don't skip your blood tests. Avoid alcohol completely if you have fatty liver, hepatitis B or C, abnormal liver tests, diabetes with obesity, or if you're on high-dose methotrexate for cancer. And never let a night out lead to a dosing mistake: low-dose methotrexate is taken once a *week*, not once a day.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and guidance on methotrexate and alcohol. It is not a substitute for the doctor or pharmacist who knows your diagnosis, dose, blood results, and other medicines. **Talk to your doctor before drinking on methotrexate**, and **contact your doctor promptly if** you notice yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, pain under your right ribs, unusual bruising or bleeding, fever, sore throat or mouth ulcers, or a new dry cough or shortness of breath. If you think you've taken methotrexate on more days than prescribed, call your doctor or Poison Control (1-800-222-1222 in the US) right away. In an emergency, call 911.

## Why Methotrexate and Alcohol Are a Concern: The Liver Story in Plain Words

Methotrexate is one of the most widely used long-term treatments for inflammatory conditions. At low doses (usually somewhere between 7.5 and 25 mg, taken once a week as tablets or an injection), it calms an overactive immune system. It's used for rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, psoriasis, and sometimes Crohn's disease and other conditions. At much higher doses, given in hospital, it's a chemotherapy drug. Those are very different situations, and this guide focuses mainly on the low-dose weekly version most people search about.

Methotrexate works by blocking the way cells use **folate** (a B vitamin). That slows down fast-dividing cells and dampens inflammation. It also explains most of its side effects, which is why most people on it also take a folic acid supplement.

The concern with alcohol comes down to one organ: the **liver**.

### What methotrexate does to the liver over time

When you take methotrexate, some of it gets taken up by liver cells and converted into a longer-lasting form (called polyglutamates). These can build up inside liver cells over months of treatment. In a small share of long-term users, this slow build-up contributes to:

- **Raised liver enzymes** on blood tests. This is common and often mild. It usually settles if the dose is adjusted or the folic acid is increased.
- **Fatty change and inflammation** in the liver.
- **Fibrosis**, meaning scarring of the liver tissue, and in rare cases, **cirrhosis**, which is advanced scarring that doesn't fully reverse.

The tricky part is that fibrosis can develop without any symptoms and sometimes without big changes in routine blood tests. That's why your prescriber monitors your liver regularly and pays close attention to anything else that might be stressing it.

### What alcohol adds

Alcohol is the most common cause of liver damage on its own. The liver breaks it down into **acetaldehyde**, a toxic chemical that irritates liver cells. Regular drinking leads to fat building up in the liver, then inflammation, then scarring in some people. That's the same path methotrexate can push the liver down.

So the problem isn't a dramatic chemical reaction in the moment. It's **two things that can each scar the liver, adding to each other over months and years**. Doctors describe alcohol as one of the strongest risk factors for methotrexate liver toxicity, alongside obesity, type 2 diabetes, fatty liver disease, and viral hepatitis.

### A few other overlaps

Liver damage is the main concern, but alcohol and methotrexate overlap in a few other ways too:

- **Folate.** Methotrexate blocks folate, and heavy drinking lowers folate levels through poor absorption and poor diet. Low folate makes methotrexate side effects like mouth ulcers, nausea, and blood count changes more likely.
- **Blood counts.** Methotrexate can lower white cells, red cells, and platelets. Heavy drinking can also suppress the bone marrow. This is mainly a concern with heavy, regular drinking.
- **The stomach.** Both can cause nausea and stomach upset. Many people already feel queasy the day after their methotrexate dose.
- **Infections.** Methotrexate dampens the immune system, and heavy drinking does too. Together they may make it harder to fight off infections.

## Can You Drink Alcohol on Methotrexate? What the Guidance Actually Says

You'll see two very different answers online: "never drink a drop" and "a few drinks a week is fine." Both come from real medical sources, which is part of the confusion. Here's where the main positions stand.

**Older advice: avoid alcohol completely.** For many years, the standard teaching was that anyone on methotrexate should not drink at all. A lot of patient leaflets and pharmacy labels still say this. It's the simplest and most cautious rule.

**Rheumatology guidance has relaxed somewhat.** The British Society for Rheumatology's guideline on monitoring disease-modifying drugs, published in 2017, takes the position that alcohol on methotrexate is acceptable in moderation, within national drinking limits. In the UK, that limit is **14 units a week**, spread over several days. A UK unit is 8 grams of alcohol, so 14 units works out to about 8 US standard drinks a week in total. Many rheumatology teams in the UK and elsewhere now advise patients to stay well within that number rather than ban alcohol outright.

**The data behind the more relaxed view.** A large UK study published in the *Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases* in 2017 followed people with rheumatoid arthritis who were starting methotrexate and looked at how much they drank. People drinking more than 14 units a week had a clearly higher risk of developing raised liver enzymes. People drinking within that limit showed little or no extra risk compared with non-drinkers. It's an observational study, so it can't prove cause and effect, and raised enzymes aren't the same as scarring. But it's one of the better sources of real-world data on this question, and it supports the idea that the amount matters a lot.

**Dermatology guidance tends to be stricter.** People taking methotrexate for psoriasis have historically been considered at higher risk of liver problems than people with rheumatoid arthritis. That's partly because psoriasis is linked with obesity, diabetes, fatty liver, and higher alcohol intake. The joint guidelines from the American Academy of Dermatology and the National Psoriasis Foundation list alcohol use as a key risk factor and generally advise keeping it to a minimum or avoiding it. If you're on methotrexate for your skin, expect your dermatologist to be more cautious.

**High-dose methotrexate for cancer is different again.** If you're receiving methotrexate as chemotherapy, it's given at much higher doses with careful monitoring, and the usual advice is to avoid alcohol during treatment. Follow your oncology team's instructions.

The practical takeaway: **there is no single rule that fits everyone.** Your prescriber decides based on your condition, your dose, your liver tests, your weight, your other conditions, and your drinking history. Ask them directly for a number.

## How Much Alcohol Is Okay on Methotrexate?

These are general figures to help you have an informed conversation with your doctor. They are not personal limits.

| Situation | General guidance |
|---|---|
| Low-dose weekly methotrexate, normal liver tests, no other liver risk factors | Many rheumatologists accept light drinking within national limits (in the UK, up to 14 units, about 8 US standard drinks, a week). Many advise staying well under that. |
| Methotrexate for psoriasis | Often stricter. Dermatology guidance lists alcohol as a major risk factor and tends to favor minimal or no drinking. |
| Fatty liver, hepatitis B or C, raised liver enzymes, obesity with diabetes | Usually advised to avoid alcohol. Ask your prescriber. |
| High-dose methotrexate (cancer treatment) | Avoid alcohol during treatment unless your oncology team tells you otherwise. |
| Any binge drinking (several drinks in one session) | Not recommended on methotrexate, whatever your weekly total. |

A few practical points:

- **The weekly total matters more than any single drink.** Liver risk from methotrexate builds up over time, so what you drink across weeks and months is what counts.
- **Spread it out and keep it light.** One drink on a couple of evenings is very different for your liver from five drinks on a Saturday night, even if the weekly total looks similar.
- **Know your drink sizes.** A large glass of wine or a strong craft beer can easily be two or three units. Our guide to [alcohol content by drink](/never-hungover/alcohol-content-by-drink) can help you count honestly.
- **Tell your doctor the real number.** Your prescriber uses your drinking history to decide how often to check your blood and whether your dose is safe. Underreporting it only makes their decisions less accurate.

## Can You Drink on the Day You Take Methotrexate?

There's no strong evidence that skipping alcohol only on your dose day protects your liver. The liver risk is cumulative, so it depends on your overall pattern rather than the exact timing of a drink.

That said, many people find it sensible to avoid alcohol on the day they take methotrexate and the day after, for practical reasons:

- **Nausea and tiredness peak around then.** Many people feel washed out, foggy, or queasy for a day or so after their dose. Adding alcohol usually makes that worse.
- **It's easier to keep your routine straight.** Keeping your dose day alcohol-free makes it less likely you'll forget a dose, double up, or take it at the wrong time.

Some people choose to take methotrexate on a Friday or Saturday evening so the after-effects land on a day off. If you do that, it's worth thinking about whether that's also the day you're most likely to drink, and whether to move one or the other. Ask your doctor before changing your dose day.

## The Methotrexate "Hangover" Is Real, and Alcohol Makes It Worse

If you search "methotrexate hangover," you'll find plenty of people describing the same thing: a day or two after the weekly dose with nausea, fatigue, headache, brain fog, and a general feeling of being run down. Some people call it "methotrexate fog." It happens even without any alcohol.

This matters for two reasons:

1. **It can feel like a hangover on top of a hangover.** If you drink near your dose day, the two sets of symptoms stack. It can be hard to tell which is which.
2. **There are fixes that help, and alcohol isn't one of them.** If the after-dose symptoms are getting you down, talk to your prescriber. Common options include adjusting the folic acid dose or timing, switching from tablets to injections (which some people tolerate better), changing the time of day you take your dose, or using an anti-nausea medicine. Don't try to "push through" with a drink or self-adjust your dose.

## Methotrexate, Alcohol, and Psoriasis

People with psoriasis face a bit of a double bind. Studies have consistently linked psoriasis with higher rates of drinking, and alcohol itself is thought to be a trigger that can make psoriasis flare or respond less well to treatment. At the same time, people with psoriasis are more likely to have other liver risk factors, such as fatty liver disease, obesity, and diabetes.

That combination is why dermatologists are often more cautious about alcohol and methotrexate than rheumatologists. If you're treating psoriasis with methotrexate:

- Expect your dermatologist to recommend minimal or no alcohol.
- Expect regular liver monitoring. Some clinics also use non-invasive scans (such as a FibroScan) or specific blood tests to check for scarring if you have extra risk factors.
- Be aware that cutting back on alcohol may help your skin as well as your liver.

## How Long After Stopping Methotrexate Can You Drink?

There's no official waiting period. Methotrexate leaves your bloodstream within days, but the longer-lasting form stored in liver cells can hang around for weeks or longer. Your liver may also need time to recover if your tests were abnormal.

Sensible principles:

- **Ask your prescriber**, especially if you stopped because of a liver problem or abnormal results. In that case, they may want follow-up tests before you drink again.
- **If you're stopping temporarily** (for an infection or surgery, for example), the usual alcohol advice for methotrexate still applies, because you'll be restarting soon.
- **If you're stopping to try for a baby**, follow your doctor's specific guidance. Methotrexate must be stopped well before conception, and your care team will also give advice on alcohol in pregnancy.

## The Dosing-Error Risk Nobody Mentions

This is a safety point that's easy to overlook. Low-dose methotrexate is taken **once a week**. Taking it every day by mistake is a known, serious medication error. Patient safety organizations and drug regulators have repeatedly warned about it because daily dosing can cause severe, even fatal, toxicity.

Alcohol makes mistakes more likely. If you've been drinking, you're more likely to forget whether you've taken your dose, take it twice, or grab the wrong bottle. A few simple habits help:

- Take your dose on the same day each week, at the same time, ideally on a day you're not drinking.
- Use a pill organizer or phone reminder that shows the weekly dose clearly.
- If you're unsure whether you've taken it, don't take another. Call your pharmacist or prescriber for advice.
- If you think you've taken extra doses, call your doctor or Poison Control (1-800-222-1222 in the US) right away, even if you feel fine.

## Other Medicines to Watch When You Drink on Methotrexate

When people have a hangover, they reach for painkillers. On methotrexate, that deserves a little care.

- **Ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin (NSAIDs).** Many people with arthritis take an NSAID alongside low-dose methotrexate under medical supervision, and that's generally considered acceptable. But NSAIDs can reduce how quickly the kidneys clear methotrexate, and alcohol and dehydration can stress the kidneys and stomach too. Don't add extra NSAIDs on top of your usual plan without checking. Our guide on [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) covers the stomach and kidney side.
- **Acetaminophen (Tylenol).** Usually fine at normal doses, but it's processed by the liver, which is already the organ you're protecting. Stick to the label and count every product that contains it. See our guide on [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol).
- **Trimethoprim and co-trimoxazole (Bactrim, Septra).** These antibiotics can interact dangerously with methotrexate by adding to its folate-blocking effect. Always remind any prescriber that you're on methotrexate before starting a new antibiotic.
- **Prednisone.** Many people with inflammatory arthritis take steroids at some point. Alcohol has its own interactions with them, covered in our guide on [prednisone and alcohol](/never-hungover/prednisone-and-alcohol).

A pharmacist can review your full list in a few minutes. For a wider look at how supplements and medicines interact, see our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025).

## When to Contact Your Doctor

Most people on low-dose methotrexate never have a serious problem, and regular blood tests catch most issues early. But some symptoms need attention, and some need it fast.

> **Contact your doctor promptly if you notice:**
> - Yellowing of the skin or whites of the eyes, dark urine, or pale stools
> - Pain or tenderness under the right side of your ribs
> - Unusual bruising, bleeding gums, nosebleeds, or tiny red spots on the skin
> - Fever, chills, sore throat, or any sign of infection
> - Mouth ulcers that are new or getting worse
> - A new dry cough, shortness of breath, or chest discomfort (methotrexate can rarely inflame the lungs)
> - Severe or persistent vomiting or diarrhea, especially if you can't keep fluids down
>
> **Get emergency help (call 911) for** severe shortness of breath, vomiting blood, black or tarry stools, confusion, or if you think you've taken methotrexate daily instead of weekly.

If a regular blood test comes back with raised liver enzymes, your doctor may lower your dose, pause treatment, increase your folic acid, or ask you to cut back on alcohol. Being honest about your drinking helps them pick the right fix.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

You're at higher risk from the methotrexate-and-alcohol combination if you:

- Have **fatty liver disease**, hepatitis B or C, or a history of abnormal liver tests
- Have **obesity, type 2 diabetes**, or high triglycerides
- Have been on methotrexate for **several years** or at a high cumulative dose
- Take methotrexate for **psoriasis**, where liver risk factors are more common
- Have **reduced kidney function**, which slows the clearance of methotrexate
- **Drink more than a few drinks a week**, or tend to have several drinks in one sitting

If any of these describe you, it's worth a direct conversation with your prescriber about whether you should drink at all.

## Protecting Your Liver While You're on Methotrexate

The steps that actually help are simple and well supported:

- **Keep alcohol low, or skip it,** based on your doctor's advice.
- **Take your folic acid exactly as prescribed.** It reduces many side effects, including some of the liver enzyme rises.
- **Go to every blood test.** Monitoring is how problems get caught early, while they're still reversible.
- **Manage your weight and blood sugar** if you can, since fatty liver adds to methotrexate risk.
- **Check before starting any supplement.** Some herbal products can affect the liver or interact with medicines. Tell your prescriber what you take.

On days you do drink, the usual habits for a lighter morning still apply: eat first, alternate with water, drink slowly, and stop earlier than you think you need to. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

Some people on methotrexate wonder whether a liver-support supplement could offset the risk of drinking. Here's the honest picture.

**DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the evidence comes from animal and lab studies, with a small amount of human data, including a 2015 randomized trial in people with fatty liver disease that found improvements in some liver markers. That's promising, but it's not proof.

What matters most for you:

- **There is no good evidence that DHM protects against methotrexate liver damage**, and it doesn't make it safe to drink more on methotrexate.
- **DHM hasn't been studied in people taking methotrexate**, so its interaction with the drug is not known. Ask your prescriber or pharmacist before adding it, or any other supplement.
- **It doesn't replace your monitoring, your folic acid, or your doctor's alcohol advice.**

Any supplement decision on methotrexate belongs with your prescriber, who knows your liver tests. Don't add DHM or any liver-support product on your own, and don't treat one as permission to drink more.

## The Bottom Line

- Methotrexate and alcohol can both damage the liver, and the risk builds up over time without symptoms.
- Many rheumatologists now accept light drinking within national limits for people on low-dose weekly methotrexate with normal liver tests. Dermatology guidance and many individual doctors are stricter.
- The weekly total and avoiding binges matter most. A UK study linked drinking more than 14 units a week with a clearly higher risk of raised liver enzymes.
- Avoid alcohol if you have fatty liver, hepatitis, abnormal liver tests, or are on high-dose methotrexate for cancer.
- Keep your dose day alcohol-free if you can, take your folic acid, never miss a blood test, and never take methotrexate daily by mistake.
- Ask your prescriber for a specific number. It's the most useful answer you'll get.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking methotrexate?**

It depends on your prescriber, your condition, and your liver health. Many rheumatologists accept light drinking within national limits (in the UK, up to 14 units, about 8 US standard drinks, a week) for people on low-dose weekly methotrexate whose liver tests are normal. Others, especially dermatologists treating psoriasis, prefer minimal or no alcohol. If you have fatty liver, hepatitis, or abnormal liver tests, you'll usually be advised not to drink. Ask your prescriber for a specific limit.

**How much alcohol can I drink on methotrexate?**

There's no single safe amount for everyone. UK rheumatology guidance accepts drinking within the national limit of 14 units a week, spread over several days, and a 2017 UK study found the risk of raised liver enzymes went up clearly above that level. Many doctors advise staying well under it and never binge drinking. Your own limit should come from your prescriber, who knows your liver tests and other risk factors.

**Why is alcohol bad with methotrexate?**

Both methotrexate and alcohol can damage the liver over time, causing fat build-up, inflammation, and in some people scarring (fibrosis). The effects add together, and the damage can develop without symptoms. Alcohol can also lower folate levels, which makes methotrexate side effects like mouth ulcers and blood count changes more likely.

**Can I drink on the day I take methotrexate?**

There's no strong evidence that timing your drinks around your dose day protects your liver, because the liver risk depends on your overall drinking pattern. But many people find it sensible to avoid alcohol on their dose day and the day after, since nausea and tiredness from methotrexate tend to peak then, and it lowers the chance of a dosing mistake.

**Does alcohol make the methotrexate hangover worse?**

Usually, yes. Many people feel nauseous, tired, and foggy for a day or two after their weekly dose even without drinking. Adding alcohol tends to stack a second set of similar symptoms on top. If the after-dose symptoms are bothering you, talk to your prescriber about options such as adjusting folic acid, switching to injections, or changing your dose time.

**How long after stopping methotrexate can I drink alcohol?**

There's no official waiting period. Methotrexate clears the blood within days, but a longer-lasting form can stay in liver cells for weeks. If you stopped because of abnormal liver tests, your doctor may want follow-up results before you drink again. Ask your prescriber what's right for your situation.

**What are the signs of liver damage on methotrexate?**

Early liver changes often cause no symptoms, which is why regular blood tests matter. Signs that need prompt medical attention include yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, pale stools, pain under the right ribs, unusual tiredness, and easy bruising. Contact your doctor promptly if you notice any of these.

**Does DHM protect your liver on methotrexate?**

There is no good evidence that DHM protects against methotrexate liver damage, and it hasn't been studied in people taking methotrexate. It doesn't make drinking on methotrexate safer. DHM has promising research on alcohol metabolism and liver health, mostly from animal studies with limited human data. Ask your prescriber or pharmacist before adding any supplement.
